title: Variables and Binding
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates understand that Python names are rebindable references to typed objects, not fixed-type slots like in C/Java.

phases.goal: Establish what a Python variable is and that types are not declared on names.

must_hit.point: A variable is a name bound to a value; assignment uses =.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says a variable is a name attached to a value via =, not a typed storage slot.

must_hit.point: Python is dynamically typed: a variable's type is inferred from the assigned value and is never declared.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts a = 5 with invalid int a = 5 and states types are not declared up front.

must_hit.point: None is Python's null value — a literal meaning no value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls None the null/no-value literal and notes assigning it alone prints nothing.

probes: What does it mean that Python is dynamically typed?
What is None, and what happens if you only assign it?

hints.1: Think about whether you write a type next to the name when you assign.
hints.2: Compare valid a = 5 with the C/Java-style declaration shown as contrast.
hints.3: Type comes from the value; None means no value and assigning it does not print by itself.

phases.goal: Explain how names rebind at runtime and what happens when a name was never bound.

must_hit.point: The same name may be rebound to a value of a completely different type during a program's life — dynamic binding.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks through a bound first to an integer then to a string and names this freedom dynamic binding.

must_hit.point: The type lives on the object itself, not on the name; a name is like a sticky name tag that can be moved between objects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the sticky name-tag vs fixed-bucket analogy and says type is on the object.

must_hit.point: Referring to a name that was never assigned raises NameError, and execution stops at the failing line.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States NameError for an unbound bare name and that later lines never run.

probes: Can you reassign the same variable to a different type? What is that called?
What happens if you evaluate a name that was never assigned?

hints.1: Ask where the type lives — on the name or on the object.
hints.2: Describe moving the name tag from one object to another, then what a never-bound name does.
hints.3: Binding can change at runtime (dynamic binding); an unbound name raises NameError and stops execution.

phases.goal: Contrast Python's rebindable names with fixed-type variables in statically typed languages.

must_hit.point: In C or Java a variable is like a fixed plastic bucket that only accepts one declared type; in Python a variable is a sticky name tag that can be moved to a differently typed object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Retells the bucket vs sticky name-tag analogy and ties it to where type lives.

must_hit.point: Statically typed languages force you to declare the type up front; Python never declares the type on the name.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says int a = 5 is the static contrast and is not valid Python; Python infers from the value.

probes: How do Python variables differ from variables in C or Java?
Why is int a = 5 shown in the notes if it is not valid Python?

hints.1: Picture a bucket that only holds one kind of thing versus a movable label.
hints.2: Separate the name from the object: who owns the type in each model?
hints.3: C/Java: fixed typed slot declared up front; Python: rebindable name, type on the object.

phases.goal: Apply binding rules to reassignment and unbound-name errors in real snippets.

must_hit.point: You can assign a number to a name and then assign a string to the same name; Python does not complain — it rebinds the name to the new object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes rebinding from a number to a string and that Python simply moves the name.

must_hit.point: Evaluating a bare unbound name is an error, not a silent no-op; later assignments and prints after that line never run.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the NameError trap and that execution stops so later statements do not execute.

probes: Walk through assigning a number then a string to the same name — what happens?
If the first line is a bare unbound name, do later assignment and print lines still run?

hints.1: Trace what the name points to after each assignment.
hints.2: For the error case, ask whether Python skips the bad line or stops.
hints.3: Rebind silently across types; unbound bare name → NameError and nothing after it runs.

tradeoffs.topic: Sticky name tag (Python) vs fixed typed bucket (C/Java)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: In C/Java the variable is a fixed-type slot (bucket) that rejects the wrong kind of value; in Python the name is a sticky tag you can peel off one object and slap onto another, so the type lives on the object and the binding can change at runtime.
Static languages force a type declaration up front (as in int a = 5); Python never declares the type on the name — the type is inferred from the value assigned, and that binding can later change.

gotchas.trap: Evaluating a bare name that has not been bound is a silent no-op or just leaves the name as None.
gotchas.correction: It raises NameError, and execution stops at that line — later assignments and prints never run.

gotchas.trap: Thinking int a = 5 is valid Python because it shows a typed variable.
gotchas.correction: That form is only a contrast with statically typed languages; it is not valid Python syntax.

gotchas.trap: Expecting assigning None to print or show something by itself.
gotchas.correction: None means no value; assigning it does not print anything on its own.
